notes: Ruling slot 22 = Voltaic Armed Forces under Lamizana (military rule since 3 Jan 1966); coalition slot 13 = Garango's technocratic finance administration. UDV-RDA placed in slot 20 following MD (RDA lineage, slot has starting popularity). MLN moved from MD's slot 3 to 18 (African socialism, slot with popularity). MD sprite BFA_Nat_Autocracy_small belongs to the later CDP, so not reused.

0.name: Les fidèles de Koudougou
0.text:
Les fidèles de Koudougou are the loyalists of Maurice Yaméogo, first president of Upper Volta, overthrown by the general strike and army intervention of 3 January 1966. Yaméogo was tried in 1969 for embezzlement and sits in prison, but his kinsmen and clients in Koudougou and the old one-party apparatus remain bitter and organised.

They want a strong presidency, close alignment with France and Côte d'Ivoire, generous French aid and a political class freed from union and student agitation. Anti-communist and personalist, they see Lamizana's austerity as a betrayal of the country's friends. Their leverage lies in Yaméogo's home region and in sympathisers in Abidjan.

1.name: Archidiocèse de Ouagadougou
1.text:
The Archdiocese of Ouagadougou heads the Catholic Church in Upper Volta, led since 1960 by Archbishop Paul Zoungrana, created a cardinal in 1965. Its missions, schools and catechists form the best-organised civil network in the country, and its former pupils fill the civil service, the unions and the officer corps.

The Church supports moral order, social Catholic reform, mission education and moderate, pro-Western government, and it welcomed the 1966 transition as a defence against disorder. It is wary of Marxist students and of Muslim reformism alike. Its leverage lies in schools, Christian unions and the voice of the pulpit across the Mossi plateau.

2.name: Parti du regroupement africain
2.text:
The African Regroupment Party is the Voltaic section of the federalist party launched by Léopold Sédar Senghor's allies in 1958, rooted in Bobo-Dioulasso and the west. The western opposition's best-known figure, Nazi Boni, exiled under Yaméogo, returned after 1966 but died in a road accident in 1969, and the party now prepares for the promised return of elections.

It stands for multiparty government, regional balance against Mossi predominance, civil liberties and close but critical ties with France within a West African federation. Its base lies among western peoples, Bobo merchants and teachers. Its leverage comes from being the main alternative to the UDV-RDA.

3.name: Les syndicats du 3 janvier
3.text:
Les syndicats du 3 janvier are the trade-union centres whose general strike and street demonstrations brought down Maurice Yaméogo on 3 January 1966 and handed power to the army. Christian, socialist and independent federations of teachers, civil servants and railway workers have since become the strongest civil force in Ouagadougou.

They defend wages, union freedom, a fair civil-service budget and an early return to civilian, parliamentary government, and they bristle at Lamizana's salary cuts. Mostly moderate and attached to French and international labour links, they bargain hard with the regime. Their leverage lies in the general strike, which has already toppled one president.

4.name: Parti africain de l'indépendance
4.text:
The African Independence Party is the clandestine Marxist-Leninist party of Upper Volta, organised in the early 1960s as the local branch of the PAI founded in Senegal in 1957. Never legal, it works through teachers, students and young civil servants in Ouagadougou and Bobo-Dioulasso, and its members are active in the unions that toppled Yaméogo.

It calls for a national democratic revolution, nationalisation of trade, land reform and an end to French economic tutelage, and it looks to the Soviet Union as the natural ally of African liberation. Its leverage lies in the trade-union and teachers' movements, where its disciplined cells punch far above their size.

5.name: Union générale des étudiants voltaïques
5.text:
The General Union of Voltaic Students gathers Voltaic students in Dakar, Abidjan and France and belongs to the Federation of Black African Students in France (FEANF). With higher education at home barely begun, its members study abroad, where they absorb the radical anti-imperialism of the Latin Quarter after May 1968.

It condemns the military regime, French tutelage and the franc zone, and demands a revolutionary transformation of Voltaic society; its members argue between pro-Soviet, pro-Chinese and Trotskyist lines. Its leverage lies in the future elite it is training and in the pressure it can bring through unions and schools at home.

6.name: Les Nkrumahistes
6.text:
Les Nkrumahistes are Voltaic admirers of Kwame Nkrumah, the Ghanaian leader overthrown in February 1966 who now lives in exile in Conakry. Teachers, former migrants to Ghana and veterans of the anti-colonial left, they remember the 1961 customs union with Ghana and see the Mossi plateau as part of a wider Africa betrayed by pro-Western rulers.

They demand a united Africa, a break with the franc zone and French tutelage, and authoritarian discipline in the service of the nation. Hostile to Washington and Paris, they look to the anti-imperialist camp for support. Their leverage lies in migrant networks reaching into Ghana and in the radical wings of unions and schools.

7.name: Les jeunes capitaines
7.text:
Les jeunes capitaines are the junior officers and cadets of the Voltaic army, trained in France, Madagascar and elsewhere, who resent the senior officers around Lamizana and the old politicians waiting to return. They admire Nasser and the Algerian army and talk of a revolution made from the barracks.

They want an army that purges corruption, mobilises the peasantry and ends dependence on France, even at the price of authoritarian rule and new friendships with radical states. For now they are scattered and lack a leader of stature. Their leverage lies in the troops they command and in the army's established habit of intervening in politics.

8.name: Les commerçants libanais
8.text:
Les commerçants libanais are the Lebanese merchant families of Ouagadougou and Bobo-Dioulasso, many of them Shia from south Lebanon, who dominate wholesale trade, transport and import houses. Holding French or Lebanese passports, they keep out of Voltaic politics while financing mosques and charities in their home villages.

Their religious leanings follow the reformist message of Imam Musa al-Sadr, who seeks the support of the West African diaspora for Lebanon's Shia. They want stable government, low taxes, safe property and good relations with whoever rules. Their leverage lies in credit, import licences and a business network linking Abidjan, Accra and Beirut.

9.name: La Husayniyya de Bobo
9.text:
La Husayniyya de Bobo is a small prayer and mourning circle of Lebanese Shia families in Bobo-Dioulasso, where young men taught by Najaf-trained clerics lead the Muharram commemorations. It stands apart from the wealthier notables of the community, whom it accuses of neglecting faith for commerce.

Its members hold that learned jurists should guide the community in all matters, public and private, and regard Western culture as corrupting. Politically insignificant in Upper Volta, they focus on religious education and on events in Iraq and Lebanon. Their leverage lies in family remittances and the respect owed to clerical learning.

10.name: Communauté musulmane de Haute-Volta
10.text:
The Muslim Community of Upper Volta is the national association of imams, marabouts and Muslim notables founded in 1962 to represent the country's Muslims before the state. Led by senior imams of Ouagadougou and Bobo-Dioulasso, it brings together Tijani and Qadiri networks and keeps good relations with every government.

It is quietist and loyal: it seeks recognition, Koranic schools, pilgrimage places and a fair share of public posts beside the Catholic elite, without challenging the secular state. It welcomes aid from Saudi Arabia and Egypt. Its leverage lies in the Friday mosques and in the quiet influence of Muslim traders and chiefs.

11.name: Ahl al-Hijra
11.text:
Ahl al-Hijra, the people of the emigration, is a small circle of young Voltaic Muslims back from study in Medina, Cairo and Mauritania who preach in market mosques against both the marabouts and the secular state. They take their model from the West African jihads of Usman dan Fodio and El Hadj Omar.

They argue that only a caliphate ruled by the sharia can abolish idolatry, colonial borders and Western law, and they denounce the Muslim Community as servants of the government. They are few and watched by the police. Their leverage lies in the prestige of Arabic learning and in growing frustration among poor Muslim youth.

12.name: Les réformistes de la Sunna
12.text:
Les réformistes de la Sunna are Muslim reformers, many of them Dyula and Hausa traders and returned students, who have begun building their own mosques in Ouagadougou and Bobo-Dioulasso. They reject the veneration of saints and costly ceremonies, and follow the modernist Islam taught in Cairo and Medina.

They want modern Franco-Arabic schools, Islamic morality in public life and Muslim participation in politics through legal channels, while respecting the constitutional order. They are wary of both the Catholic elite and the Sufi establishment. Their leverage lies in traders' money and in an educated youth seeking a faith fit for city life.

13.name: La Garangose
13.text:
La Garangose is Ouagadougou's name for the austerity regime of Finance Minister Tiémoko Marc Garango, an army quartermaster officer who has served Lamizana since 1966. Through salary cuts, tax increases and strict budget control, his technocrats have restored the public finances wrecked under Yaméogo and become the true managers of the state.

They stand for balanced budgets, honest administration and development without debt, above party politics and loyal to the military government rather than to any foreign bloc. Civil servants grumble, but donors approve. Their leverage lies in control of the treasury, the ministries and the timetable of the promised constitutional transition.

14.name: Les chefs de canton
14.text:
Les chefs de canton are the customary chiefs of the Voltaic countryside, Mossi, Gourmantché, Gurunsi and Bobo, who collect taxes, settle disputes and deliver votes under every regime since colonial times. Weakened by Yaméogo's attacks on chieftaincy, they have regained influence under the military, which needs them to govern the villages.

They stand for rural order, respect for custom, land held by lineages and a cautious, non-aligned government that leaves the countryside alone. They distrust urban unions and students. Their leverage lies in their hold over the peasantry, the vast majority of the population, and in the votes they can bring to any party that courts them.

15.name: Chambre de commerce de Haute-Volta
15.english: Chamber of Commerce of Upper Volta
15.text:
The Chamber of Commerce of Upper Volta brings together the French import houses, Lebanese wholesalers and leading Voltaic merchants of Ouagadougou and Bobo-Dioulasso. It speaks for the trading firms that handle cattle, cotton and groundnut exports and the flow of goods along the Abidjan–Niger railway.

It wants low taxes, cheap credit, protection of property and stable ties with Côte d'Ivoire and France, and it watches Garango's austerity with mixed feelings. Pragmatic, it supports any government that keeps the railway open and the franc stable. Its leverage lies in credit, customs revenue and the import trade on which the state budget depends.

16.name: Les Dioula
16.text:
Les Dioula are the independent Muslim traders, transporters and artisans of Bobo-Dioulasso, Ouagadougou and the market towns, heirs to the long-distance Dyula commerce of the Niger bend. They run kola, cloth and cattle trade across the borders with Ghana, Mali and Côte d'Ivoire, often outside official channels.

They want free markets, low duties, open borders and as little state as possible, and they resent price controls, customs officers and the big import houses alike. They have no party, but their purses fund candidates and mosques. Their leverage lies in controlling the everyday trade in food and goods.

17.name: Groupements Naam
17.text:
The Naam Groups are village self-help associations founded in 1967 in Yatenga by the teacher and rural organiser Bernard Lédéa Ouédraogo, who adapted the traditional kombi-naam youth work groups to modern development. They organise young farmers to build stone lines, plant trees, dig wells and run cereal banks against hunger.

They stand for development from below, protection of soil and water against the advancing Sahel, and peasant dignity rather than projects imposed by the state or foreigners. Non-aligned and apolitical, they nonetheless challenge the chiefs' monopoly in the villages. Their leverage lies in the spread of their groups across the northern plateau.

18.name: Mouvement de libération nationale
18.text:
The National Liberation Movement is the pan-Africanist socialist party founded in 1958 by the historian Joseph Ki-Zerbo, banned under Yaméogo and strong among teachers, students and union militants. Ki-Zerbo played a key part in the January 1966 uprising, and the movement now prepares to contest elections once constitutional rule returns.

It stands for African unity, a non-aligned foreign policy, planned rural development, universal education and an end to neo-colonial dependence, without adopting Soviet communism. Its base lies in the educated urban class, especially teachers. Its leverage lies in ideas, in Ki-Zerbo's prestige and in its close links with the unions.

19.name: La Ligne de Pékin
19.text:
La Ligne de Pékin is the pro-Chinese tendency among Voltaic students and young teachers, formed in the FEANF and in student hostels in Dakar and Paris after the Sino-Soviet split. It reads Mao on peasant revolution and accuses the PAI of following Moscow's revisionism and of courting the military.

It wants a people's war rooted in the peasantry of the Mossi plateau, the overthrow of chiefs and compradors, and complete independence from both superpowers. Small and secretive, its cells argue as much among themselves as with the regime. Its leverage lies in its students, future teachers who will carry the line into the schools.

20.name: Union démocratique voltaïque–Rassemblement démocratique africain
20.text:
The Voltaic Democratic Union–African Democratic Rally is the former ruling party, the Voltaic branch of Félix Houphouët-Boigny's RDA, which governed as a single party under Maurice Yaméogo until 1966. Distancing itself from Yaméogo and led by figures such as Gérard Kango Ouédraogo and Joseph Ouédraogo, it remains the largest political machine in the country.

It combines Mossi-based mass nationalism, patronage and support for the chiefs with a pro-French, pro-Ivorian outlook and free enterprise. Its leverage lies in the countryside, where its local committees survived the suspension of party politics, and in Lamizana's need for a partner in any return to civilian government.

21.name: Le pouvoir kaki
21.text:
Le pouvoir kaki is the name given to the officers who want the army to keep power indefinitely rather than hand it back to the politicians removed in 1966. Concentrated in the general staff and the garrison commands, they see parties and unions as the source of disorder and corruption.

They want a permanent military regime, a single national movement under army control, censorship and harsh discipline, justified by a nationalism that places the army above tribe and religion. They distrust Western liberalism and Marxist radicals alike. Their leverage lies in command of the troops and in Lamizana's dependence on their loyalty.

22.name: Forces armées voltaïques
22.text:
The Voltaic Armed Forces have ruled Upper Volta since 3 January 1966, when Lieutenant-Colonel Sangoulé Lamizana, the army chief of staff, took power at the call of the crowds and unions that brought down Maurice Yaméogo. Now a general, Lamizana governs as head of state and head of government through a mixed military and civilian cabinet.

The army presents itself as an arbiter above parties, restoring public finances and preparing a constitution that will share power with elected civilians while keeping officers in government. Pro-French but cautious, it relies on French aid and technical assistance. Its leverage is decisive: it holds the state.

23.name: Mogho Naaba
23.text:
The Mogho Naaba is the king of the Mossi of Ouagadougou, the senior sovereign of the Mossi kingdoms that dominate central Upper Volta. Mogho Naaba Kougri, on the throne since 1957, tried in October 1958 to force a constitutional monarchy by surrounding the territorial assembly with his followers, but failed, and the republic has since kept the court out of formal power.

The court stands for Mossi tradition, the hierarchy of chiefs, respect for custom and a monarchy embedded in the state. Its ministers and chiefs still command deep loyalty across the plateau. Its leverage lies in that loyalty, which every party and every general must court.
